title: Bronchiectasis: a neglected lung disease steps out of the shadows
summary: Bronchiectasis is more common than once thought, often missed for years, and only now getting its first dedicated medicine and new guidelines. Most of its causes, including tuberculosis, are concentrated in low- and middle-income countries, where care is hardest to reach.
body:
Bronchiectasis was long treated as a rare disease of the past. Today it is recognised as a common, chronic lung condition that is growing worldwide, often missed for years, and only now getting its first dedicated medicine and modern guidelines. For people in low- and middle-income countries, where most of its causes are concentrated, the gap is widest.

## What is bronchiectasis?

In bronchiectasis, the airways of the lungs become permanently widened and scarred. Mucus collects instead of being cleared, bacteria settle in, and the result is a cycle of inflammation, infection and further damage.

Typical signs include:

- a cough with phlegm on most days
- chest infections that keep coming back
- breathlessness and tiredness
- sometimes, coughing up blood

It can follow severe pneumonia, tuberculosis (TB) or whooping cough, and is linked to immune problems, COPD, asthma and other conditions. In many people no single cause is found.

## More common, and more often missed, than we thought

Over the past few decades bronchiectasis has moved from being seen as an orphan disease to a recognised global problem, with incidence and prevalence rising in many countries. Part of that rise reflects better access to CT scans, which are needed to confirm the diagnosis.

Estimates still vary enormously, from around 50 to more than 1,000 cases per 100,000 people depending on the country and study, and experts agree the disease is underdiagnosed in many parts of the world. Getting a diagnosis can take a long time: speakers at the 2026 European Respiratory Society Congress cited delays of roughly 3.5 to 17 years from first symptoms.

## A turning point for treatment

For decades, care relied on airway-clearance physiotherapy, antibiotics for flare-ups and long-term options used off label. That is starting to change.

- **A first dedicated medicine.** Brensocatib (Brinsupri), an oral tablet that targets the inflammation driving the disease, became the first approved treatment for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis in the United States in August 2025, followed by the European Union in November 2025, the United Kingdom and, in 2026, Japan. In the ASPEN trial, the largest bronchiectasis trial to date, it reduced the yearly rate of flare-ups by about a fifth compared with placebo.
- **New guidelines.** The European Respiratory Society updated its bronchiectasis guidelines in 2025, and the American College of Chest Physicians published the first North American guideline in July 2026.

These are real advances. But they mostly reach patients in high-income health systems.

## The global gap

Most of what we know about bronchiectasis comes from Europe, North America and Australasia. Yet the conditions that most often cause it, including severe lung infections in childhood and tuberculosis, are far more common in low- and middle-income countries. Researchers warn that findings from high-income settings cannot simply be transferred, and that post-TB lung disease in particular remains underestimated and under-reported.

Many people whose TB has been "successfully treated" go on to live with damaged lungs, frequent infections and breathlessness, with no follow-up and no lung-health care. In many districts, the CT scans needed to confirm bronchiectasis, sputum testing and physiotherapy are simply not available.

## What countries can do

GALA Health calls on health authorities to:

- **Count it.** Include bronchiectasis and post-TB lung disease in national NCD and chronic respiratory disease plans, and record them in health information systems.
- **Link TB and lung-health care.** Check lung function and symptoms at the end of TB treatment, and refer people with ongoing problems.
- **Make basic care available close to home.** Airway-clearance techniques, vaccination against flu and pneumococcus, prompt treatment of flare-ups and pulmonary rehabilitation are low-cost and effective.
- **Build diagnostic capacity.** Plan access to CT imaging and sputum culture at referral level, and train primary care teams to recognise the signs.
- **Plan for fair access to new medicines** as they are approved, so that innovation does not widen the gap between countries.

## Know the signs

A cough with phlegm most days, or chest infections that keep coming back, are not something to put up with. If that sounds familiar, talk to a doctor or nurse. You can also take our free 2-minute [Lung Check](https://galahealth.org/lungcheck), and read how [Barbara found support living with bronchiectasis and COPD](https://galahealth.org/voices) on our Voices page.

## Sources

- [Bronchiectasis epidemiology review, European Respiratory Review (2024)](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/errev/33/174/240091)
- [Bronchiectasis in low- and middle-income countries, European Respiratory Journal editorial (2023)](https://publications.ersnet.org/content/erj/61/1/2201977)
- [Diagnostic delays and exacerbation burden in Europe, ERS Congress 2026 symposium, EMJ Respiratory](https://www.emjreviews.com/respiratory/symposium/updates-in-bronchiectasis-diagnostic-delays-and-exacerbation-burden-in-europe-j16126/)
- [FDA approval of brensocatib, AJMC (August 2025)](https://www.ajmc.com/view/brensocatib-becomes-first-fda-approved-therapy-for-bronchiectasis)
- [MHRA licenses brensocatib, UK Government](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/brensocatib-licensed-as-the-first-medicine-specifically-designed-to-treat-non-cystic-fibrosis-bronchiectasis-in-patients-12-years-and-older)
- [Brensocatib launches in Japan, AJMC (October 2026)](https://www.ajmc.com/view/brensocatib-launches-in-japan-for-non-cf-bronchiectasis)
- [ERS and CHEST guidelines compared, Managed Healthcare Executive (October 2026)](https://www.managedhealthcareexecutive.com/view/bronchiectasis-recommendations-american-vs-european-chest-2026)

This article is for general information and is not medical advice.

title: World COPD Day 2026: Finding COPD early is the first step to a better life
summary: COPD is now the world's third leading cause of death, yet most people living with it have never been diagnosed. This World COPD Day, we look at why early diagnosis matters and what countries can do.
body:
This Wednesday, 18 November, is World COPD Day. The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) has chosen the theme **"Early Diagnosis and Management for a Better Life."** The message is simple: improving diagnosis and starting treatment earlier can lead to a better life, with fewer symptoms and slower progression of the disease.

The burden is enormous. According to the World Health Organization, COPD is now the third leading cause of death worldwide, with 3.4 million deaths in 2023 — about 6% of all deaths globally. The impact is deeply unequal: nearly 90% of COPD deaths in people under 70 occur in low- and middle-income countries.

## A disease hiding in plain sight

COPD develops slowly. Breathlessness on the stairs, a morning cough or more frequent chest infections are easy to put down to age, smoking or "just a cold". As a result, most people with COPD are never told they have it. In a major international study covering 27 countries, more than 80% of COPD cases identified by spirometry were undiagnosed — and in some sites the figure was close to 100%.

Part of the reason is access. COPD is confirmed with spirometry, a simple breathing test, but spirometry is often unavailable in low- and middle-income countries, so the disease is easily missed. Even when it is diagnosed, treatment is not guaranteed: in 2023, salbutamol inhalers were generally available in public primary care in fewer than two-thirds of low and lower-middle income countries.

## Not only a smokers' disease

Tobacco remains the leading preventable cause of COPD, but it is far from the whole story. WHO estimates that smoking causes over 70% of COPD cases in high-income countries, but only 30–40% in low- and middle-income countries, where household air pollution from cooking and heating with biomass fuel or coal is a major risk factor. Occupational dust and fumes, childhood respiratory infections and childhood asthma also play a part. Women cooking over open fires and workers in dusty jobs are at real risk — and are often the least likely to be tested.

## Why early diagnosis changes everything

COPD cannot be cured, but it can be managed well. Symptoms can improve with treatment and lifestyle changes; bronchodilator inhalers are the main treatment, and pulmonary rehabilitation improves breathing and exercise ability. Quitting smoking, avoiding indoor smoke, staying active and getting vaccinated against flu, pneumonia and COVID-19 all help. The earlier these steps begin, the more lung function, independence and quality of life people keep — for themselves and for the families who so often carry the daily burden of care.

## What countries can do

At GALA Health, we see early diagnosis as a health-system question, not only a clinical one. Countries can make rapid progress by:

- bringing spirometry and trained staff into primary care, not only specialist hospitals;
- actively checking people at high risk — smokers, people exposed to biomass smoke, workers in dusty occupations — rather than waiting for symptoms to become severe;
- making essential inhalers affordable and reliably available;
- including pulmonary rehabilitation and COPD care in Universal Health Coverage benefit packages;
- building COPD into national NCD investment cases, so it is funded, measured and scaled.

Because what is not prioritized is not funded, and what is not funded does not scale.

## Join World COPD Day

GOLD will release its updated global COPD strategy, the GOLD 2027 report, on World COPD Day. We encourage partners, health professionals and families to share the campaign using **#WorldCOPDDay**, and to visit our [Respiratory Health Calendar](campaigns.html#world-copd-day) for our key messages and share kit.

If you have ever been short of breath and wondered why, ask your doctor about a breathing test.

**Sources:** [WHO COPD fact sheet](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/chronic-obstructive-pulmonary-disease-%28copd%29); [GOLD, World COPD Day 2026](https://goldcopd.org/); Lamprecht B. et al., Determinants of underdiagnosis of COPD in national and international surveys, [Chest 2015](https://doi.org/10.1378/chest.14-2535).

title: Why Chronic Respiratory Disease Needs to Be a Global Health Priority
summary: Chronic respiratory diseases cause millions of deaths a year — most of them in countries with the least capacity to respond. Here's why that gap defines GALA Health's work.
body:
Chronic respiratory diseases — asthma, COPD, and related conditions — remain one of the most under-recognized categories of global disease burden. They cause close to 4 million deaths a year, and the impact falls disproportionately on low- and middle-income countries, where the vast majority of COPD deaths in people under 70 occur, according to the World Health Organization.

This is not primarily a medical gap. Effective prevention and treatment for chronic respiratory disease exist. What's missing, in most affected countries, is integration: national health systems that account for lung health in financing, diagnostics, and care pathways in the way they already do for other major disease categories.

GALA Health works to close that gap. Our approach is country-led, evidence-driven, and partnership-based — we provide technical assistance and policy advisory support to help governments build chronic respiratory disease care into the systems they already own, rather than proposing solutions built for them from the outside.

That includes work on prevention (indoor and outdoor air pollution, urban planning), access (diagnostics, essential medicines, insurance coverage), and a part of the picture too often left out of policy entirely: support for the informal caregivers who carry much of the daily burden of chronic respiratory disease at home.

What is not prioritized is not funded. What is not funded does not scale. Changing that is the work.
